The True Hall of Fame — the same yardstick for every player who ever played.

Ranked on the field, not on ballots.

Welcome to The True Hall Of Fame — a virtual hall for the MLB players whose careers, measured by the statistics they piled up, put them among the best ever to play the game. Membership is decided by a single formula built from box-score facts: a player's Stat Above Average (SAA), the same calculation applied to everyone. There's no five-year waiting period and no requirement to be retired — active players are eligible. Every player here earned the ticket on the field.

The museum in Cooperstown, New York is a wonderful place — artifacts from every era and a gallery of plaques for the players voted in. And that's the operative word: voted. Induction is an honor decided by ballot, with the writers and the era committees weighing each candidate and casting a yes or a no. That's a legitimate way to run a hall of fame, it's the one they chose, and they've never claimed the vote is beyond dispute. But a ballot is a judgment call, and judgment varies — from writer to writer, and from one era's standards to the next. In our view, that has left the results inconsistent enough to be worth a second look on the numbers alone. Some of what that looks like:

Hank Aaron was elected in his first year on the ballot, as he should have been — but not unanimously. He was named on 406 of 415 ballots, 97.8%. Nine writers left the game's all-time home run leader off entirely. Willie Mays drew 94.7%. Ted Williams, 93.4%. You can argue any single omission; it's harder to explain why the inner-circle greats face meaningful opposition at all.

The first player ever elected unanimously wasn't Babe Ruth, Ty Cobb, or Walter Johnson. It was Mariano Rivera, in 2019. Of everyone in the Hall, exactly one has been named on every ballot. One.

And the voting doesn't track production cleanly. Bobby Grich (71.1 career WAR) and Lou Whitaker (75.1) are on the outside looking in, while Harold Baines (38.7) and Tommy McCarthy (14.7) are in.

None of this makes Cooperstown wrong — it's their hall, run their way, by rules they're entitled to set. But in our view the process is broken in a specific way: it's inconsistent, and it shifts with who is voting and when. So we built the other version — one transparent formula, applied identically to every player in history, with no ballots and no committees. That's The True Hall of Fame.

The True Hall of Fame — hitters, part one of two

Top 300 Hitters by Stat Above Average

This isn't trying to reproduce who's actually in Cooperstown — it's this project's own answer to who belongs. No linear-weight run values, no replacement-level constant: every player is scored against the league he actually played in, season by season and tilted toward his own position, using five genuinely separate skills — batting average, isolated power, walk rate, stolen-base rate, and fielding.

1,065qualifying pool
300shown here
5,000+career PA minimum
149 / 300also in Cooperstown

This is a living ranking, not a set of plaques. It's rebuilt from scratch every year on the latest data, so a player climbs onto the list when his case passes the 300th, and a borderline name drops off when someone else's rises past him. Active players are in — no five-year wait. What you're looking at is the 2025 edition; the twenty names just outside the cut are listed at the bottom.

What's a Stat Above Average? Each player-season is compared to its own season — a 1927 season is judged against 1927, a 2024 season against 2024, nothing crosses eras. The five inputs above are each converted to a z-score (standard deviations above or below the bar for that year, computed from qualifying hitters only) and blended into one number for the season: batting average and isolated power at 30% each, defense at 20%, walk rate and stolen-base rate at 10% each. (Walks and steals are both dialed back — a walks-only bat or a pure basestealer could each otherwise ride one category onto the list ahead of a complete hitter; leaning the score on contact and power pulls the list closer to the actual Hall of Fame.) The defensive input is Baseball-Reference's Fielding Runs for the season — the one number here that isn't a plain box-score rate, because fielding doesn't have one.

The bar leans toward your position. A .290 shortstop and a .290 first baseman are not the same player, but scored against the whole league they look identical — and that quietly buried the great up-the-middle names (Ripken, Larkin, Bench) far below where they belong. So the four bat-and-legs categories are measured against a bar set 60% of the way from the league average toward the average for the player's own position that season. Fielding Runs are position-relative by nature — a shortstop's are already measured only against other shortstops.

The career number blends length and peak. A player's season scores, each scaled to a 600-PA workload, are summed into a career total — with below-average seasons counted at 40% weight, so a few years too long in the league dings a great career without erasing it. A great career cut short shouldn't be buried under compilers either, so the ranking metric is the average of that career total and the sum of the player's best seven seasons (the same career-plus-peak shape JAWS uses). Play a long time and at a high level and both halves are large.

Negro Leagues players qualify on a separate standard, not the 5,000 PA floor — their official league schedules were far shorter than MLB's, and the surviving record undercounts them further still. They qualify instead by accumulating the equivalent of 9 seasons at their own league's typical season size — the standard that gets Josh Gibson, Willie Wells, and Turkey Stearnes onto this list. The NeL flag beside a player's rank marks the ones whose score actually draws on Negro Leagues play — a 200-plus-PA season in a Negro Major League — not a brief cameo like Willie Mays's 13 games in 1948.

Runs scored and RBI were deliberately left out — both depend heavily on who's on base ahead of you and where you hit in the order, not just your own output. The HOF column marks players the writers and veterans committees have already voted into Cooperstown, so you can see at a glance where this list and the official one agree and where they don't.

Where the list and your gut disagree

Two it leaves out

Nellie Fox and Don Mattingly are two names most fans would swear are already on a list like this — an MVP apiece, nineteen All-Star nods between them — and the formula leaves both off, for opposite reasons. Fox, 357th, is a Hall of Famer whose whole case is glove and bat-to-ball with nothing else attached. Mattingly, 310th, ran fifteen years on the writers' ballot without getting in; his problem here is the reverse of Fox's — a great bat, and not much career around it.

#357 Nellie Fox 2B · 1947–1965 · CHW

.288 AVG · 94 OPS+ · 2,663 H · 35 HR · 719 BB · 49.3 bWAR

AVG+0.65
ISO-0.94
BB-0.68
SB-0.20
DEF+1.36

The glove is the real thing — +1.36, three Gold Gloves, the best defensive second baseman of his era by Baseball-Reference's Fielding Runs — and he put the ball in play as well as anyone alive, leading the league in hits four times and almost never striking out (+0.65 on average). But there is nothing else. No power at all (−0.94, the bottom of the board), a walk rate below his own league (−0.68), and a park-adjusted OPS of 94 — a career of slightly below-average hitting. SAA leans 60% of the bat score on average and power together, so a glove-and-slap infielder with a hole where the secondary skills go has no way up the list. The 1959 MVP, and 357th here.

#310 Don Mattingly 1B · 1982–1995 · NYY

.307 AVG · 127 OPS+ · 2,153 H · 222 HR · 1,099 RBI · 42.4 bWAR

AVG+1.21
ISO+0.22
BB-0.62
SB-0.61
DEF-0.64

+1.21 on contact — a genuine batting-title bat, and the 1985 MVP — with a touch of power on top. Around it, gaps: he didn't walk much (−0.62), never ran, and the defense grades negative (−0.64) despite nine Gold Gloves, because first base carries a steep positional discount — the glove saved runs, but the bar for the position is low. And the peak, as good as any bat in the game from 1984 to 1989, is basically the career: a back injury turned him ordinary at 29 and finished him at 34. His best seven seasons actually outscore his career total — the sign of a player the years were too few for. A great hitter, a low-value position, thirteen seasons: 310th, and the closest thing on this list to the Hall's own long argument about him.

At 149 of the 300, this is the closest the list has come to Cooperstown. Scoring the bat against the position — and, since the 2025 pass, taking defense straight from Baseball-Reference's Fielding Runs — closed most of the old gap at catcher and up the middle: Johnny Bench (40th), Iván Rodríguez (68th), Alan Trammell (71st), Luis Aparicio (170th) and Ozzie Smith (179th) all sit inside now. What it still won't do is bend for a career built almost entirely on the glove — Bill Mazeroski (722nd), Omar Vizquel (422nd), Rabbit Maranville (436th). That's the point.

Recalculated every year

On the bubble

The twenty just outside the cut, ranks 301–320. A strong season from an active player, a shift in the Negro Leagues record, or the next weighting pass, and the line moves.

SAA = a weighted blend of five per-season z-scores — batting average [H/AB] and isolated power [SLG−AVG] at 30% each, defense [Baseball-Reference Fielding Runs: range + catcher defense + the positional adjustment] at 20%, walk rate [BB/PA] and stolen-base rate [SB/PA] at 10% each — against that season's mean and spread among 200+ PA hitters, the bar for the four bat-and-legs stats set 60% of the way toward the player's own position. Each season is scaled to 600 PA; below-average seasons are counted at 40% weight in the career total. The ranking number is the average of the career total and the sum of the player's best seven seasons. Pool: 5,000+ career PA (or, for Negro Leagues players, 9+ seasons normalized to their own league's typical season size). Source: Lahman database hitting (2025 release, including Negro Leagues statistics) and Baseball-Reference Fielding Runs; Hall of Fame membership current through the 2026 induction class.

How Stat Above Average works

One formula, applied identically whether you struck people out or drove them in.

A hitter's Stat Above Average (SAA) is built one season at a time. Each season, four rate stats and a fielding number are turned into z-scores — standard deviations above or below the bar for that season, measured against qualifying hitters only — then blended by weight, scaled to a 600‑plate‑appearance workload, and summed across the career. The bar is mostly the league, but tilted toward the player's own position; a below-average season is dampened before it's added in. Both adjustments are explained under the formula. The ranking number is a JAWS-style 50/50 average of that career total and the sum of the player's seven best individual seasons, so a long steady career and a short brilliant one can both build a real case.

Hitters = 30% AVG vs league & position + 30% ISO vs league & position + 20% Defense vs position + 10% Walk rate vs league & position + 10% Steal rate vs league & position

A pitcher's SAA works the same way, minus the peak adjustment: five z-scored rate stats per season (ERA and WHIP flipped, so beating the league counts as positive), blended by weight, scaled to a 200‑inning workload, and summed across every qualifying season. There is no best-seven bonus — a pitcher's number is the career total only.

Pitchers = 25% ERA vs league + 25% WHIP vs league + 20% K/9 vs league + 20% Win% + 10% Saves vs league

Every comparison is to the player's own contemporaries in the exact seasons he played — a 1927 season is judged against 1927, a 2024 season against 2024. A career that spans eras gets a benchmark blended across those years. Nothing is measured against a fixed all-time standard or a replacement‑level constant. The weights are deliberately tilted toward contact, power, and run prevention: a walks-only bat or a pure basestealer could otherwise ride a single category past a complete player.

The bar bends toward your position. A good-hitting shortstop still looks ordinary next to a league full of first basemen and corner outfielders, which for years buried the great up-the-middle players — the Ripkens, the Larkins, the Benches — a hundred spots too low. So the four bat-and-legs categories aren't scored against the whole league anymore. Each is measured against a bar set 60% of the way from the league average toward the average for the player's own position (shortstop, second base, catcher, and so on) that season. Defense was always judged this way. Held fully to position it would swing too far the other way — telling the formula a no-hit shortstop is "average" and floating good gloves with empty bats up the list — so it lands at 60%.

Hanging on doesn't erase what came before. Because every season is scored against the league, a below-average year comes out negative and eats into the career total — which quietly penalizes a great player for sticking around a few years past his prime. Those sub-average seasons still count, but at 40% weight in the career total. The peak half of the formula — the seven best seasons — never includes them anyway.

Glossary

Every abbreviation you'll run into on the lists, the cards, and the Stats pages.

The five hitting inputs

AVG — Batting average
Hits divided by at‑bats. The oldest measure of pure contact.
ISO — Isolated power
Slugging percentage minus batting average: extra bases per at‑bat, with singles stripped out. A hitter with nothing but singles has an ISO of .000; prime Babe Ruth sat around .350.
Defense (Fielding Runs)
Baseball‑Reference's Fielding Runs for the season — range in the field, catcher defense (throwing, framing, blocking), small good‑play adjustments, and the positional adjustment that values a shortstop's spot above a first baseman's and docks a designated hitter for not taking one. Divided by games and scored against the league like the other four. This is the one SAA input that isn't a plain rate stat: fielding has no clean box‑score number, so SAA borrows a real one rather than build a worse substitute. Earlier editions used a home‑made putout‑and‑assist range figure that couldn't see catcher defense at all.
Walk rate (BB)
Bases on balls as a share of plate appearances — how often a hitter reaches base without putting the ball in play.
Steal rate (SB)
Net stolen‑base value per plate appearance: steals credited, caught‑stealing charged at a heavier penalty. Weighted lightly on purpose.

The five pitching inputs

ERA — Earned run average
Earned runs allowed per nine innings. Lower is better, so the z‑score is flipped before it's blended.
WHIP — Walks and hits per inning pitched
Baserunners allowed per inning, walks plus hits. Also flipped — fewer is better.
K/9 — Strikeouts per nine innings
The one bat‑missing skill that shows up on every stat sheet, in any era.
Win% — Winning percentage
Wins divided by decisions (wins plus losses). It leans on the team around the pitcher, so it carries a modest weight.
SV — Saves
Games finished protecting a lead, per the official rule. Weighted lightest of the five: it depends heavily on how a manager chooses to use a pitcher.

Other batting stats on the site

OBP — On‑base percentage
Times reached base (hits + walks + hit‑by‑pitch) divided by plate appearances.
SLG — Slugging percentage
Total bases divided by at‑bats — a double counts 2, a home run 4.
OPS — On‑base plus slugging
OBP + SLG. A quick catch‑all for offensive value; .900 and up is star level.
OPS+ — Adjusted OPS
OPS restated so 100 is league average and each point above is one percent better, adjusted for ballpark. 150 means 50% better than league.
PA — Plate appearances
Every trip to the plate, walks and sacrifices included. SAA scales each hitting season to 600 PA.
R, RBI, HR, H, 2B, 3B, SB, BB, SO
Runs, runs batted in, home runs, hits, doubles, triples, stolen bases, walks, strikeouts — raw season and career totals, no adjustment.

Other pitching stats on the site

IP — Innings pitched
Shown in the traditional thirds notation: 200.1 is 200 innings and one out, 200.2 is two outs. SAA scales each pitching season to 200 IP.
ERA+ — Adjusted ERA
ERA restated to a 100‑is‑average, park‑adjusted scale where higher is better — the inverse direction of raw ERA.
W, L, G, GS, CG, SHO
Wins, losses, games, games started, complete games, shutouts.
H, ER, HR, BB, SO (allowed)
Hits, earned runs, home runs, walks, and strikeouts a pitcher gave up.

Methodology terms

z‑score
How far a number sits from the average, measured in standard deviations. A z of +1 is one standard deviation better than that season's qualifying players; +2 is rare air. SAA blends z‑scores, not raw stats, so separating yourself in a tightly bunched category counts for more than in one where the league is spread all over.
“vs league” / league‑relative
Every rate input is scored against the average of the same season, never a fixed all‑time bar. This is the core difference from career‑counting totals and from WAR's replacement level. (The defensive input starts from Baseball‑Reference's Fielding Runs, then that too is scored against the season's league.)
“vs position” / position‑relative
The bar an input is scored against is nudged toward the average for the player's own fielding position that season, so a shortstop's bat is measured mostly against other shortstops. Batting average, isolated power, walk rate and steal rate are 60% of the way there, 40% still whole‑league. Defense is inherently position‑relative — a shortstop's Fielding Runs already compare him only to other shortstops, plus the positional adjustment for playing the harder spot.
Decline‑season weighting
A qualifying season that grades out below average scores negative, which subtracts from the career total. Those negative seasons are cut to 40% weight before they're added in, so a long tail of past‑prime years dings a great career without gutting it. The peak component is untouched.
Qualifying season
A season that counts toward SAA: 200+ plate appearances for a hitter, 40+ innings for a pitcher. Below the line, a season doesn't move the number.
Peak / best‑seven
For hitters, the final SAA is a 50/50 average of the career total and the sum of the seven best individual seasons — the same idea as Baseball‑Reference's JAWS. It stops a compiler with no great years from outranking a shorter‑career great. Pitchers get no peak component.
WAR / bWAR
Wins Above Replacement, the mainstream all‑in‑one value stat. “bWAR” is Baseball‑Reference's version, the one quoted on this site. See Why not WAR? below.
Replacement level
The baseline WAR measures against: what a team could get essentially for free from the minor leagues or the waiver wire. SAA has no equivalent — it compares to the real league, not a hypothetical floor.
NeL
A flag on the lists marking a player whose SAA draws on Negro Leagues seasons — now part of the official record and scored exactly the same way.
Cooperstown / HOF
The Baseball Hall of Fame in Cooperstown, New York, and its membership, which is decided by vote. The HOF column on each list shows who is already in.

Why not WAR?

Wins Above Replacement measures every player against one universal "replacement level" — a theoretical bench player, calibrated once from decades of injury-substitution data and then applied identically to a dead-ball-era outfielder and a modern closer. It's the industry standard for good reason, but that one number was never derived for either of them specifically.

Stat Above Average measures every player against their own competition instead — the actual league average, in the actual years and at the actual position they played, blended across whichever eras their career spans.

No replacement level. No runs-to-wins conversion. No linear-weight run values turning a double into a decimal. Just each player's rate stats, held up against the players who were actually on the field around them — with one exception: fielding has no clean rate stat, so the defensive input starts from Baseball-Reference's Fielding Runs before being scored against the league like everything else.

Different question, different answer — but not a wildly different one. The Credibility page lays SAA next to WAR, WAA, and JAWS across the whole pool: where they line up, where they part ways, and the reason behind every gap.
